blocks.text: Order of Advent of Europeans in India 1. Portuguese (1498)

The Portuguese came to India for various economic and religious reasons. They were the first to introduce tobacco and cashew nuts in India. They were the first to arrive and the last to leave. Goa was liberated in 1961.
Vasco da Gama (1498)
Vasco da Gama was the first to discover the sea route to India via the Cape of Good Hope.
He was a Portuguese explorer who came to Calicut in 1498 during the rule of King Zamorin (then Hindu ruler).
+ He reached Calicut aboard the Portuguese ship Sao Gabriel, guided by an Arab navigator named Ahmad ibn Majid (Ibn Majid).

Treaty of Tordesillas, signed on 7th June 1494 was a significant agreement between Spain and Portugal. It aimed to resolve conflicts over newly discovered lands by dividing the world into two spheres of influence. The treaty established a demarcation line, with lands to the east belonging to Portugal and lands to the west to Spain.
Francisco de Almeida (1505)
He was the first Portuguese Viceroy of India.
He brought "Blue Water Policy" (Cartaz System) which was a trade licensing system that allowed the Portuguese to control trade in Indian Ocean.
Afonso de Albuquerque (1509)
He was the second Portuguese Governor of India. He is considered as the real founder of Portuguese power.
He captured Goa in 1510 (from Adil Shah of Bijapur) and abolished Sati. '
He received permission to build a fort at Bhatkal from Krishnadevaraya.
He was a Portuguese Governor who moved capital from Cochin to Goa in 1530.
Bahadur Shah, ruler of Gujarat surrendered Diu to Portuguese 'in 1535. A har DUTCH Arrival of Dutch
Dutch refers to "people from Netherlands".
Dutch East India Company was formed in 1602.
They set up their first factory in Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) in Andhra Pradesh in 1605.
1599: East India Company came into existence.
1600: East India Company received a Royal Charter from Queen Elizabeth I to trade in India.
1608: William Hawkins was sent by King James I of England and arrived at the court of Jahangir.
1611: First factory at Masulipatnam (temporary).
1613: First factory at Surat (permanent).
1615: Sir Thomas Roe visited the court of Jahangir (arriving on the English ship Hector) to obtain official trading rights for the English East India Company.
1620: Danes established their first factory at Tranquebar (Tamil Nadu).
1668: French established their first factory at Surat.
Battle of Swally/Suvali (1612): Fought in Surat. The British defeated the Portuguese.
+ Battle of Chinsurah/Bedara/Hooghly (1759): Fought on the banks of the Hooghly River. The British defeated the Dutch.
Battle of Colachel in 1741 between Marthanda Varma (King of Travancore) and Dutch East India Company. The Dutch were defeated.
The series of Carnatic Wars started between British and French East India Companies.
A total of 3 Carnatic Wars were fought between 1744 and
Dupleix\ed the French forces in the first two Carnatic Wars.
1st Carnatic War (1744-1748)
Extension of the Austrian War of Succession.
Battle of Adyar (1746) is also called the Battle of St. Thome.
It ended with Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.
Won by: French East India Company.
It started with Battle of Ambur (1749) was won by the French forces led by Joseph Francois Dupleix, supporting Chanda Sahib.
+ It ended with Treaty of Pondicherry.
Note: Dupleix led French forces in the first two wars.
3rd Carnatic War (1756-1763)
Battle of Wandiwash (1760) was a part of 3rd Carnatic War.
+ This war was an extension of Anglo-French War of 7 years which was caused by Austrian War of Succession.
It ended with Treaty of Paris.
+ British forces led by Sir Eyre Coote defeated the French forces led by Comte de Lally.
Result: French were limited to their enclaves (Pondicherry, etc.) and no further expansion was allowed.
1717-1727: Murshid Quli Khan served as the first Nawab of Bengal.

In 1717, Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar issued a Golden Farman (Magna Carta of Trade) that allowed the British East India Company to trade freely in Bengal for a yearly payment of 3,000 Rupees. The farman also granted the company the right to issue Dastaks, or trade permits, to move goods.
Murshid Quli Khan — Shuja-ud-Din Muhammad Khan > Alivardi Khan (died in: 1756) — Siraj-ud-Daulah Siraj-ud-Daulah
He became the Nawab at the age
of 23 years after the death of Alivardi
Khan in 1756.
He was the last self-governing
He was not happy with the Trade privileges enjoyed by Britishers in Bengal.

Siraj-ud-Daulah, captured the Fort William after the British refused to stop fortifying it. The Black Hole Tragedy was a night of captivity for British soldiers and other prisoners in a small, airless room in Fort William, Calcutta in 1756.
This incident instigated Robert Clive, who decided to take revenge, which led to the Battle of Plassey.
Treaty of Alinagar (1757) ee:
'It was signed between Siraj-ud-Daulah and the Britisher which became the cause of Battle of Plassey.
It was fought between the East India Company force led by Robert Clive and Siraj-ud-Daulah (Nawab of Bengal).
Mir Jafar, the military commander of Siraj-ud-Daulah joined hands with the Britishers.
This battle confirmed the formal beginning of British Empire in India.
Outcomes of Battle of Plassey
Siraj-Ud-Daulah was killed (forces led by Mir Madan).
Mir Jafar was made the new puppet Nawab of Bengal.
Then Mughal Emperor: Alamgir II.
Subsequently, Mir Qasim (son-in-law of Mir Jafar) came to the throne. He shifted the capital from Murshidabad to Munger (he also ended Dastak issued by Farrukhsiyar).
Combined forces Shuja-ud-daulah (Nawab of Awadh), Mir Qasim and Shah Alam II (Mughal Emperor) led to Battle of Buxar (1764) against the Britishers.
1st Nawab of Awadh: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk.
The fourth Nawab of Awadh — Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula, built Bara Imambara in Lucknow.
Battle of Buxar (1764)
Britishers won this battle led by Hector Munro.
Treaty of Allahabad was signed in 1765 between Shuja- ud-Daula (Nawab of Awadh), Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II and was negotiated by Robert Clive on behalf of the East India Company.
Under this, two separate treaty were signed.
First Treaty with Nawab of Awadh:
Allahabad and Kara were 3 A · Shah Alam U handed over to Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. oH - Robert Clive
Nawab paid Rs 50 lakh to the British as war indemnity. SESE TICES OIL EE Second Treaty with Shah Alam II:
Emperor Shah Alam II was placed under British protection at Allahabad.
Diwani (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa were given to the East India Company, in return of an annual payment of Rs 26 lakh.

The Company was to receive Rs 53 lakh from the Emperor for performing nizamat (military and judicial) functions in these provinces. This control over Diwani and Nizamat Functions by East India Company is called as Dual Government in Bengal.
Mir Jafar was made the Nawab again.
Allahabad Treaty ran for 7 years and was ended by Warren Hastings in 1772.
+ In Mysore, the Wodeyar Dynasty was ruling. Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar strengthened and consolidated the Mysore state.
Hyder Ali began his career as a soldier under the Wodeyars and gradually rose to power, eventually becoming the de facto ruler of Mysore, while the Wodeyars continued as nominal rulers.
1st Anglo-Mysore War (1767-1769)
The East India Company, Marathas, and the Nizam of Hyderabad were on one side, while Haider Ali was on the other.
It ended with the Treaty of Madras (1769), in which the British assured assistance to Haider Ali in the event of an attack by the Marathas or the Nizam.
2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-1784)
Cause: Violation of the Madras Treaty by the British.
Hyder Ali was defeated in the battle of Porto Novo (1781)
by the British forces led by Sir Eyre Coote.
Tipu Sultan sat on throne after the death of his father Hyder Ali due to cancer in the middle of the war.
There was no winner in this war. It ended with Treaty of Mangalore.
3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1790-1792)
The British were led by Lord Cornwallis.
It ended with Treaty of Seringapatnam.
Tipu Sultan was defeated in this war (Capital:
Under this treaty, a heavy war indemnity of %3 crore was imposed on Tipu Sultan.
Additionally, he had to cede half of his kingdom to the British, Marathas, and the Nizam, and two of his sons were taken as hostages.
4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798-1799)
Tipu established the Jacobin Club and declared himself "Citizen Tipu".
Heplanted the "Tree of Liberty" inhis capital, Seringapatam.
He established contact with Napoleon Bonaparte and invited him to come to India to launch a joint struggle against the British.
Due to growing proximity of Tipu Sultan with French, Britishers waged another war with him.:
Tipu Sultan was killed in the Battle.
Result: The independent power of Mysore came to an end.
The Mysore state was handed back to the Wodeyar dynasty (under British suzerainty).
British power was fully established in South India.
Subsidiary alliance was introduced by Lord Wellesley in 1798, though it was a brain-child of French Governor General Dupleix.

Under the subsidiary alliance, Indian rulers had to pay subsidy for the British Garrison and British Army deployed in their territory. They had to seek permission from British EIC to partner with any other European for any service, and also for the negotiations with other Indian rulers.
Adopted by: Hyderabad (first State to sign in 1798); Mysore (in 1799); Tanjore (in 1799); Awadh (in 1801) and Peshwa (in IN PUNJAB

Maharaja Ranjit Singh from Sukerchakia Misl (one of the 12 Sikh Misls) signed Treaty of Amritsar in 1809 with British and declared Sutlej river as boundary between the Sikh Kingdom and the British Empire.
After the death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1839), political instability spread in Punjab.
Maharaja Duleep Singh ascended the throne at a very young age.

Lord Hardinge was the Governor-General of India at this time.
Treaty of Lahore (1846) (Lahore was the capital) and Treaty of Bhairowal (1846) were signed between Maharaja Duleep Singh and British.
Treaty of Amritsar (1846): In this treaty, the British handed over the Kashmir region to Raja Gulab Singh. In exchange, Raja Gulab Singh paid %75 lakh.
It resulted in the defeat and partial subjugation of the Sikh Empire and cession of Jammu & Kashmir as a separate princely state under British suzerainty.
2nd Anglo-Sikh War (1848)
Mulraj, the Governor of Multan, was dissatisfied with British control.
In 1848, Mulraj killed two British officers of the East India Company. This incident sparked the Sikh rebellion.
Maharaja Duleep Singh was captured and sent to Britain and Kohinoor diamond was stolen. Lord Dalhousie was then Governor-General of India.

+ Background: In the 19th century, the Tsarist Empire (Russia) was expanding rapidly towards Central Asia. The British feared that Russia might attack India, which was the most important colony of the British Empire.
+ Buffer State Policy: It was considered necessary to make Afghanistan a buffer state to safeguard British India from external threats (especially Russia).
Buffer State: A state located between two powerful countries to prevent direct conflict between them.
Ring Fence Policy: Warren Hastings adopted this policy in 1765.
Objective: To create a protective ring of friendly/allied states around Company territories to safeguard them from external threats.
Nature: Defensive policy (focused on protection rather than expansion).
Forward Policy: Associated with Lord Auckland.
It was believed that if Russia advanced towards India, it was better to intervene in Afghanistan beforehand.
This policy led to British intervention in Afghanistan, resulting in the First Anglo-Afghan War.
Tripartite Treaty (1838):
The Tripartite Treaty was signed in 1838 under the Forward Policy of Lord Auckland.
This treaty was between three parties: 1. British Government
2. Shuja Shah Durrani (Afghan Ruler)
3. Ranjit Singh (Sikh Ruler)
Objective:
To remove Dost Mohammad Khan and install Shuja Shah on the throne of Afghanistan.
To bring Afghanistan under British influence.
1st Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842)
Fought during the tenure of Lord Auckland (Governor- General of India).
+ Initially, the British succeeded in removing Dost Mohammad Khan and placed Shah Shuja Durrani on the throne of Afghanistan.
However, this success was short-lived and a rebellion led to the collapse of British control.
Result: The British were defeated and forced to retreat from Kabul (1842); the retreat was nearly annihilated, marking one of the worst defeats in British Indian history.
+ Later, John Lawrence (Governor-General) adopted the Policy of Masterly Inactivity towards Afghanistan.
2nd Anglo-Afghan War (1878-1880)
Treaty of Gandamak was signed between the British Government and Afghan ruler Yakub Khan.
Afghanistan's foreign policy went under British contol
Some frontier areas were given to British India
Lord Lytton implemented the "Proud Reserve Policy" of Britain.
The Durand Line was drawn in 1893 to define the boundary between Afghanistan and British India. This laid the foundation for today's Afghanistan-Pakistan border.
Between: British India and Afghan Ruler Amir Abdur Rahman Khan.
Drawn by: Sir Mortimer Durand.
3rd Anglo-Afghan War (1919)
Occurred during the viceroyalty of Lord Chelmsford; led by Amanullah Khan, it ended with the Treaty of Rawalpindi, granting Afghanistan control over its foreign affairs.
1st Anglo Burma War (1824-1826)
It ended with the Treaty of Yandaboo (1826).
2nd Anglo Burma War (1852-1853 )
Battle of Saragarhi (1897):
The Battle of Saragarhi occurred during a tribal uprising on the North-West Frontier.
It took place in present-day Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Pakistan).
It was associated with the Tirah Campaign (1897-98).
21 soldiers of the 36th Sikh Regiment fought against thousands of tribal warriors. ~ Anglo-Nepal War (1814-1816):
The Treaty of Sugauli was signed after this war in 1816.
Through this treaty, the border between British India and Nepal was determined, and Nepal had to cede some territories.
